displayQuote: Those who dare to fail miserably can achieve greatly

meta.title: Who really said "Those who dare to fail miserably can achieve greatly"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: It isn’t John F. Kennedy. The line is a reworded version of Robert F. Kennedy’s 1966 Cape Town speech — JFK had died three years earlier.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Those who dare to fail miserably can achieve greatly'?
meta.ogDescription: Widely credited to JFK, but it’s a variant of Robert Kennedy’s 1966 Day of Affirmation line — delivered after JFK’s death.

answer.label: Not John F. Kennedy — actually Robert F. Kennedy
answer.sourceLine: The idea traces to Robert Kennedy’s Day of Affirmation Address ↗ at the University of Cape Town on 6 June 1966 — “only those who dare to fail greatly, can ever achieve greatly” — delivered two-and-a-half years after John F. Kennedy’s death. The smoother “fail miserably” wording pinned on the president is a later popular variant with no source in anything JFK said or wrote.

source.heading: The real source

docMeta.dd: University of Cape Town, South Africa · 6 June 1966
John F. Kennedy, as “dare to fail miserably”

source.excerpt: Of course to adhere to standards, to idealism, to vision in the face of immediate dangers takes great courage and takes self-confidence. But we also know that only those who dare to fail greatly, can ever achieve greatly.
trail: The words come from Robert Kennedy’s Cape Town Day of Affirmation Address ↗ of 6 June 1966: “only those who dare to fail greatly, can ever achieve greatly.”
Wikiquote ↗ files the line under RFK with the Cape Town 1966 citation, noting variants as reprinted in Ripples of Hope (2003).
Quote sites such as Goodreads ↗ still file the reworded “fail miserably” version under John F. Kennedy — flagged “not verified.”
source.cutTag: ↑ the viral JFK version rewrites ‘fail greatly’ as ‘fail miserably’, drops the ‘only’, and swaps in the wrong Kennedy
source.excerptNote: The sentence sits in RFK’s passage on courage and idealism; the freestanding “fail miserably” aphorism is a stripped-down paraphrase, not a transcript of anything either Kennedy said.

author.name: Robert F. Kennedy
author.heading: About Robert F. Kennedy
author.bio: Robert Francis Kennedy was U.S. attorney general (1961–64) under his brother John, then U.S. senator from New York (1965–68). His 1966 Day of Affirmation speech to South African students — delivered at the height of apartheid — is among his most quoted, and he was assassinated in June 1968 while seeking the Democratic presidential nomination.

copyAttribution: Robert F. Kennedy, "Day of Affirmation Address," University of Cape Town, 6 June 1966: "only those who dare to fail greatly, can ever achieve greatly." Often reworded as "dare to fail miserably" and misattributed to John F. Kennedy, who had died in 1963.

misattribution.heading: Why the JFK credit is wrong
misattribution.intro: “Those who dare to fail miserably can achieve greatly” is one of the most common Kennedy mix-ups online — the words are the wrong brother’s, and even then they’ve been reworded.

items.why: JFK was assassinated in November 1963 — more than two years before the speech that produced this line. No JFK address or writing contains it; it doesn’t appear on Wikiquote’s John F. Kennedy ↗ page in any form, yet aggregators like BrainyQuote ↗ still credit him.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is Robert F. Kennedy’s, from Cape Town on 6 June 1966 — “only those who dare to fail greatly, can ever achieve greatly” (Wikiquote ↗); “fail miserably” is a later paraphrase.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Kennedy delivered the “dare to fail greatly” line to students at the University of Cape Town during apartheid, in a speech built around the idea that ordinary acts of courage — “numberless diverse acts of courage and belief” — are what bend history. Daring to fail was framed as the price of idealism, not a slogan about ambition.
The stripped-down, motivational-poster form — and its reassignment to the more famous President Kennedy — sands off that context, turning a call to moral risk into a generic line about achievement.
detailsBody: RFK’s transcript reads “fail greatly,” not “fail miserably.” The “miserably” variant, the dropped “only,” and the switch from Robert to John Kennedy are all features of the internet-era quote, not of the 1966 record.
